title: What a function builds before it starts working
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read a prologue and say what the frame contains, recognise register spilling, and explain why optimised code often has no frame pointer at all.

blocks.text: A frame is the block of stack a function claims for itself. What goes in it is decided by three pressures: values that will not fit in registers, registers the function must give back unchanged, and anything whose address is taken.

blocks.caption: The full sequence, and what each step is for
lines: push rbp              ; save the caller's frame pointer
mov  rbp, rsp         ; establish ours
push rbx              ; save any callee-saved registers we intend to use
push r12              ;   -- one push each, in a fixed order
sub  rsp, N           ; claim N bytes for locals and spills
...the function's actual work...
add  rsp, N           ; release the locals
pop  r12              ; restore the saved registers
pop  rbx              ;   -- in exactly reverse order
pop  rbp              ; restore the caller's frame pointer
ret
/* Every step has an exact undo, and the undos run in reverse. A prologue
and epilogue that do not mirror each other is either hand-written
assembly with a bug, or a function doing something unusual on purpose. */

blocks.text: Spilling, annotated by the compiler itself

blocks.caption: A function with more live values than registers
lines: A function with ten parameters that also makes calls:
_spill:
push rbp
mov  rbp, rsp
push r15                                ; five callee-saved registers,
push r14                                ; saved because this function
push r13                                ; wants to use them and must
push r12                                ; give them back unchanged
push rbx
sub  rsp, 40                            ; then space for locals
mov  dword ptr [rbp - 68], r9d          ## 4-byte Spill
mov  dword ptr [rbp - 44], r8d          ## 4-byte Spill
mov  dword ptr [rbp - 48], edx          ## 4-byte Spill
add  rsp, 40                            ; the epilogue undoes it
pop  rbx                                ; in exactly reverse order
pop  r12
pop  r13
pop  r14
pop  r15
pop  rbp
ret
/* Those Spill comments are the compiler's own annotation: it ran out of
registers and moved values to the stack. A frame full of spills is a
function with more simultaneously live values than the sixteen
registers can hold. */

blocks.title: Spills are a readable signal about the source
blocks.text: A frame with many spills usually means a function doing too much at once: long expressions, many arguments, or a loop body holding a great deal of state. When you are optimising and see heavy spilling in a hot function, splitting it or shortening the live range of some values often helps more than any micro-optimisation of the arithmetic. The compiler has told you, in its own comments, exactly what its problem was.

blocks.caption: The stack protector, as actually emitted
lines: int leaf(int a, int b) { int t[4] = {a,b,a+b,a*b}; ... }
push rbp
mov  rbp, rsp
sub  rsp, 32
mov  rax, qword ptr [rip + ___stack_chk_guard@GOTPCREL]
mov  rax, qword ptr [rax]
mov  qword ptr [rbp - 8], rax        ; the canary, just below saved rbp
...                                  ; the array lives further down
mov  rcx, qword ptr [rip + ___stack_chk_guard@GOTPCREL]
mov  rcx, qword ptr [rcx]
cmp  rcx, qword ptr [rbp - 8]        ; still intact before returning?
Measured: this file's two array functions produce 6 stack_chk references.
A function with no local array produces 0.
/* The canary sits between the locals and the saved rbp and return address.
Anything overflowing an array upward must cross it, and the check before
ret catches the corruption. It defends the return address specifically,
which is why the compiler adds it only when a local array exists. */

blocks.text: The previous lesson explained why the return address is vulnerable. This is the standard defence, and its position in the frame is the whole design: it is placed above the locals and below the saved registers, so a linear overflow of a local buffer has to destroy it on the way to anything important. The check happens immediately before the epilogue, so corruption is detected before ret can use a corrupted address.

blocks.title: It defends against one shape of attack
blocks.text: A canary catches a contiguous overflow that runs upward from a buffer. It does not catch a write to an arbitrary computed index, an overflow that skips over the canary, or a corrupted pointer used to write elsewhere. Knowing what a mitigation actually covers is more useful than knowing it exists — the compiler's own choice not to insert one in a function without arrays makes its scope explicit.

blocks.caption: Optimised code often omits it entirely
lines: A function that:
- has a fixed frame size known at compile time, and
- does not need to take addresses relative to a stable base
does not need rbp at all. Locals are addressed from rsp instead.
With frame pointer:        Without:
push rbp                   sub  rsp, 24
mov  rbp, rsp              mov  dword ptr [rsp + 4], edi
sub  rsp, 24               ...
mov  [rbp - 20], edi       add  rsp, 24
...                        ret
add  rsp, 24
pop  rbp
ret
/* Omitting it frees a register and removes two instructions. The cost is
that a debugger can no longer walk frames by following saved rbp values,
which is why unwinding then relies on the separate .eh_frame data the
.cfi directives in compiler output produce. */

blocks.text: This is why disassembly of optimised code so often begins with sub rsp rather than push rbp, and why a backtrace from an optimised build can be wrong or incomplete when the unwind information is missing. Reading frames without a frame pointer means tracking rsp adjustments yourself, which the tooling module covers.

blocks.title: Read frames of increasing complexity
steps: Write a function with two int parameters and no locals; compile at -O1 and note the frame
Add a local array of four ints and recompile; find the canary and the larger frame
Confirm with grep that the array version references stack_chk and the first does not
Write a function with ten parameters that calls another function, and count the pushes
Identify which registers are pushed and check them against the callee-saved list
Find the compiler's own Spill comments and count them
Compile the same function at -O2 and see whether the frame pointer survives
For one frame, draw the memory layout from rbp+16 down to rsp
blocks.expected: A frame that grows with each addition, canary references appearing exactly when a local array does, pushes matching the callee-saved list, and a drawing you can check against the offsets in the code. The grep step matters: it turns 'the compiler adds a canary when there is an array' from something you were told into something you verified in one command.

cheatsheet: Prologue: push rbp ; mov rbp, rsp ; push callee-saved ; sub rsp, N
Epilogue undoes each step in exactly reverse order
The frame holds arrays, address-taken values, spills, saved registers and stack arguments
Spill comments in compiler output mean more live values than registers
Heavy spilling suggests splitting the function rather than micro-optimising it
A stack canary sits above the locals and below the saved rbp and return address
Verified: functions with a local array reference stack_chk; one without references it 0 times
A canary catches contiguous upward overflows, not arbitrary-index writes
Optimised code often omits rbp, addressing locals from rsp instead
Without a frame pointer, unwinding relies on the separate .eh_frame data

checkpoint.prompt: A prologue pushes rbp, r15, r14, r13, r12 and rbx. What does the epilogue do?

choices.A: Pops them in the same order
choices.B: Pops rbx, r12, r13, r14, r15 and rbp — exactly reverse order, because the stack is last-in first-out

checkpoint.explanation: Every prologue step has an exact undo and the undos run in reverse. A prologue and epilogue that do not mirror each other is a strong signal something unusual is happening.

checkpoint.prompt: You see many instructions the compiler annotated as 'Spill'. What does that tell you about the source function?

choices.B: It has more simultaneously live values than the sixteen registers can hold, so values were moved to the stack

checkpoint.explanation: Heavy spilling usually means the function is doing too much at once. Splitting it or shortening live ranges often helps more than optimising the arithmetic.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is the stack canary placed above the locals rather than anywhere else in the frame?

choices.B: So that a contiguous overflow running upward from a local buffer must destroy the canary before reaching the saved rbp and return address
choices.C: Because rbp-8 is the fastest address to access

checkpoint.explanation: The position is the entire design. The check runs immediately before the epilogue, so corruption is detected before ret can use a corrupted address.

checkpoint.prompt: An optimised function starts with sub rsp, 24 and never touches rbp. What has happened, and what is the cost?

choices.B: The frame pointer was omitted: locals are addressed from rsp, which frees a register — at the cost that a debugger cannot walk frames by chaining saved rbp values
choices.C: The prologue is missing due to a bug
choices.D: The function is a leaf and needs no frame

checkpoint.explanation: Unwinding then depends on the separate .eh_frame data. This is why backtraces from optimised builds can be incomplete when that information is stripped.
